summary: NASA set out on 23 October how it intends to land astronauts on the Moon in 2028; Artemis III stays a crewed orbital test, with a summer 2027 launch in view and a two-day docking with a Blue Moon test lander.
China launched the 28th group of its state low-orbit internet satellites on a Long March 8A from Hainan on 25 October, fifteen days after the 27th.
Poland's prime minister closed his India visit in Bengaluru with space named as a priority, but no POLSA and ISRO agreement had been publicly reported.
Saudi Arabia's Royal Commission for AlUla commissioned two LaserSETI stations, the network's first site in Asia.
2026-10-26.bottom_line: The weekend brought confirmation rather than new decisions: NASA kept its 2028 landing target and commercial landers at the centre of it, while China kept adding state broadband capacity. The next dated decisions are NASA's commercial station proposals on 8 December and ESA's Rome meeting on 15 December.

audio_sections.title: Opening
audio_sections.text:
Good morning. It's Monday, the twenty sixth of October, and here's what's happening in space.

NASA has laid out how it plans to get astronauts back on the Moon in twenty twenty eight. China has added another batch of satellites to its state internet network. And Poland's prime minister has wrapped up his visit to India, with space high on the agenda but no new agency deal on paper.

audio_sections.title: Top story
audio_sections.text:
The top story comes from Florida. On Friday, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and senior agency leaders gave an update on the Artemis programme at Kennedy Space Center.

The headline is that the plan hasn't changed. NASA still aims to land astronauts on the Moon in twenty twenty eight. Before that, Artemis three will fly as a crewed test in low Earth orbit, rather than going to the Moon, and officials pointed to a launch in the summer of twenty twenty seven.

The programme manager, Jeremy Parsons, explained what the crew will actually do. They'll dock with a test version of Blue Origin's Blue Moon lander and stay attached for two days, climbing inside to check life support and other key systems. It's a rehearsal for the hardware that will eventually carry people down to the surface.

There are question marks over timing, though. Isaacman told NASA staff in a memo last month that Artemis three was running about three months behind, and Bloomberg reports concern that some hardware may not be ready in time. NASA's answer, for now, is that the schedule holds.

Looking further ahead, the rovers that astronauts will drive on the Moon are set to come from two companies, Lunar Outpost and Venturi Astrolab. The bigger picture is that commercial landers, not just NASA's own rocket, now set the pace for the whole programme.

audio_sections.title: Around the world
audio_sections.text:
In China, a Long March eight A rocket lifted off from the commercial launch site on Hainan island on Sunday morning, Beijing time. According to the state news agency Xinhua, it carried the twenty eighth group of satellites for China's low orbit internet network, built by the China Academy of Space Technology.

The official notice didn't say how many satellites were on board, only the group number. The previous batch went up just fifteen days earlier. Put simply, China is building a national broadband network in orbit, batch by batch, at a steady clip. For governments weighing up where their satellite connections come from, that's now a second network of this scale taking shape, alongside SpaceX's Starlink.

In Saudi Arabia, the Royal Commission for AlUla says two LaserSETI stations are now up and running at its AlUla Manara observatory site. They watch the night sky for brief flashes of light, and the SETI Institute says they're the network's first stations anywhere in Asia. It's a small, scientific step, but it shows Saudi institutions building research capacity on the ground, as well as in orbit.

audio_sections.title: Closer to home
audio_sections.text:
In Poland, Prime Minister Donald Tusk finished his India trip in Bengaluru on Friday. He travelled with about a hundred business leaders, including the Polish Space Agency and the radar satellite company ICEYE.

Both governments said space has strong potential, and more than a dozen agreements were signed between companies at business forums in Delhi and Bengaluru. The two prime ministers also set a goal of doubling trade to twelve billion dollars by twenty thirty.

What hasn't appeared, at least not publicly, is the cooperation agreement between the Polish Space Agency and India's space agency, ISRO, which had been talked about before the trip. So the political backing is there, but the formal framework is still to come.

Polish coverage has focused on the openings for Polish space companies. The specialist site Space24 points out that ICEYE set up an Indian subsidiary in August, and cites reports that it's discussing a radar satellite constellation for India.

audio_sections.title: Industry and markets
audio_sections.text: On the business side, SpaceX has told US regulators it ended the third quarter with more than eleven thousand one hundred Starlink satellites in orbit, and that it added one point six million customers over those three months. Analysts quoted by CNBC say that, for governments looking for an alternative, there's still no ready replacement. That's the backdrop to Ukraine's recent move to explore a satellite network of its own.

audio_sections.title: The days ahead
audio_sections.text:
Looking ahead, NASA holds a virtual science town hall today on how it picks new missions. In Goa, the international committee on satellite navigation systems meets all week. Tomorrow, the Asia Pacific regional space agency forum opens in Bangkok, and the Defence in Space conference begins in London.

On Thursday, astronauts on the space station start the first of two spacewalks to fit new solar arrays. Friday is the deadline for comments on Blue Origin's request to launch up to fifty New Glenn rockets a year from Florida. The United States votes in its midterm elections on the third of November.

Further out, the European Parliament's industry committee votes on the EU Space Act on the tenth of November. NASA's commercial space station proposals are due on the eighth of December, and the European Space Agency meets in Rome on the fifteenth.

audio_sections.title: Close
audio_sections.text: That's the briefing for today. You'll find the full edition, with links to every source, on the Briefing tab. Have a good day.

Good morning.
It's Friday, October twenty third, and here's what's happening in space.
Ukraine is moving to build its own satellite network as the dispute over Starlink drags on.
Poland's Prime Minister takes a space delegation to Bengaluru today.
And NASA gives an update on its Moon plans this afternoon.
Ukraine has taken its first formal step toward a satellite network it controls itself.
On Thursday, during a visit to Kyiv by Finland's Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, Ukraine's defense ministry signed a letter of intent with two Finnish companies, Nokia and ICEYE.
It's a statement of intent rather than a contract, and it points toward a broadband network in low Earth orbit where the state owns the satellites, the ground stations and the terminals.
The timing isn't an accident.
For about a week, Ukrainian forces have dealt with limits on Starlink, the SpaceX service they rely on for battlefield communications and drones.
On Thursday President Trump said Elon Musk had put full access back.
But President Zelensky said speeds had not been restored, and Ukrainian officials say a cap on use from fast-moving platforms is still in place.
No budget or schedule has been announced for the new network.
Still, it's the clearest sign yet that governments see dependence on a single foreign provider as a security risk they want to remove.
In the United States, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman will brief at two this afternoon Eastern time, from Kennedy Space Center, on the plan to land astronauts on the Moon by twenty twenty eight.
Artemis three is now a crewed test in low Earth orbit next year, and reporting suggests it's running about ninety days behind its mid twenty twenty seven target.
In Russia, the head of Roscosmos, Dmitry Bakanov, said the first module of the Russian Orbital Station is being built at RSC Energia.
He also said Russia and China have discussed joint missions to the Moon and to Mars.
In Europe, attention moves to Rome.
This week's council of the European Space Agency discussed a path for low Earth orbit, the Moon and Mars, but it didn't adopt a plan or any new funding.
The intermediate ministerial meeting in Rome on December fifteenth is the next step, and the real program and funding decisions are left for the full ministerial council in twenty twenty eight.
In Brussels, the European Parliament's industry committee is set to vote on the EU Space Act on November tenth.
In Poland, Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi agreed on Thursday to deepen cooperation in defense, space and nuclear energy, and to double trade by twenty thirty.
Today the delegation visits Bengaluru, home of the Indian space agency, where a cooperation agreement between the two space agencies is planned.
Also in Poland, the satellite maker Creotech plans a new factory by twenty twenty nine that could build up to a hundred satellites a year, about ten times today's output.
Its chief executive warned that Europe will depend on American rockets for years to come.

And in a written reply to a member of parliament, reported this week, Deputy Minister Michał Jaros raised concerns about the cost of NASA's Artemis program, limited access for partners and a lack of transparency on its financing.
He said Poland is still interested in Artemis, but its lunar priority is Europe's Argonaut lander.
In Türkiye, Industry Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacır said the country plans to send its lunar vehicle in the first months of twenty twenty seven.
He added that work has started on a spaceport in Somalia, which he said could cut launch costs by about thirty percent.
In Uzbekistan, the space agency is reaching out to African countries ahead of the International Astronautical Congress in Samarkand in October twenty twenty eight.
It has proposed an easier visa route for delegates.
In Hungary, Polish space officials and companies held talks in Budapest with the Hungarian space industry and the HUNOR astronaut program.
They covered secure satellite communications under IRIS², a bigger role for both countries in ESA programs, and the EU's next long term budget.
Czechia, Sweden and Greece had no major new space news overnight, though Greece and Czechia both have dates coming up in the days ahead.
On the business side, Blue Origin has asked federal regulators to allow up to fifty New Glenn launches a year from Florida.
That's more than four times the current limit of twelve, and it comes five months after a New Glenn exploded on its pad.
Written comments are open until October thirtieth.
Looking ahead, NASA's Artemis update is this afternoon.
Next week brings the Von Braun Symposium in Huntsville from Monday, and two conferences on Tuesday and Wednesday, one in Toulouse on space resilience and one in London on defense in space.
On October twenty ninth, astronauts on the space station begin the first of two spacewalks to install new solar arrays, with the second set for November fifth.
Greece's public call to name its first astronaut mission closes on October thirtieth.
Czech Space Week runs from November second to the eighth.
The United States votes in its midterm elections on November third.
That's the briefing for today.

In the United States, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman will brief at two this afternoon Eastern time, from Kennedy Space Center, on the plan to land astronauts on the Moon by twenty twenty eight. Artemis three is now a crewed test in low Earth orbit next year, and reporting suggests it's running about ninety days behind its mid twenty twenty seven target.

In Russia, the head of Roscosmos, Dmitry Bakanov, said the first module of the Russian Orbital Station is being built at RSC Energia. He also said Russia and China have discussed joint missions to the Moon and to Mars.

In Europe, attention moves to Rome. This week's council of the European Space Agency discussed a path for low Earth orbit, the Moon and Mars, but it didn't adopt a plan or any new funding. The intermediate ministerial meeting in Rome on December fifteenth is the next step, and the real program and funding decisions are left for the full ministerial council in twenty twenty eight.

In Brussels, the European Parliament's industry committee is set to vote on the EU Space Act on November tenth.

In Poland, Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi agreed on Thursday to deepen cooperation in defense, space and nuclear energy, and to double trade by twenty thirty. Today the delegation visits Bengaluru, home of the Indian space agency, where a cooperation agreement between the two space agencies is planned.

Also in Poland, the satellite maker Creotech plans a new factory by twenty twenty nine that could build up to a hundred satellites a year, about ten times today's output. Its chief executive warned that Europe will depend on American rockets for years to come.

And in a written reply to a member of parliament, reported this week, Deputy Minister Michał Jaros raised concerns about the cost of NASA's Artemis program, limited access for partners and a lack of transparency on its financing. He said Poland is still interested in Artemis, but its lunar priority is Europe's Argonaut lander.

In Türkiye, Industry Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacır said the country plans to send its lunar vehicle in the first months of twenty twenty seven. He added that work has started on a spaceport in Somalia, which he said could cut launch costs by about thirty percent.

In Uzbekistan, the space agency is reaching out to African countries ahead of the International Astronautical Congress in Samarkand in October twenty twenty eight. It has proposed an easier visa route for delegates.

In Hungary, Polish space officials and companies held talks in Budapest with the Hungarian space industry and the HUNOR astronaut program. They covered secure satellite communications under IRIS², a bigger role for both countries in ESA programs, and the EU's next long term budget.

Czechia, Sweden and Greece had no major new space news overnight, though Greece and Czechia both have dates coming up in the days ahead.

On the business side, Blue Origin has asked federal regulators to allow up to fifty New Glenn launches a year from Florida. That's more than four times the current limit of twelve, and it comes five months after a New Glenn exploded on its pad. Written comments are open until October thirtieth.

Looking ahead, NASA's Artemis update is this afternoon. Next week brings the Von Braun Symposium in Huntsville from Monday, and two conferences on Tuesday and Wednesday, one in Toulouse on space resilience and one in London on defense in space.

On October twenty ninth, astronauts on the space station begin the first of two spacewalks to install new solar arrays, with the second set for November fifth. Greece's public call to name its first astronaut mission closes on October thirtieth.

Czech Space Week runs from November second to the eighth. The United States votes in its midterm elections on November third.

segments.text: Good morning.
It's Thursday, October twenty second, and here's what's happening in space.
Europe's space agency has wrapped up its council meeting in Paris with a plan for low Earth orbit, the Moon and Mars headed to ministers in Rome.
A Polish executive has been named to run the agency's commercial partnerships.
And Türkiye's new budget nearly triples its space and aviation program.
The European Space Agency's three hundred and fiftieth council met in Paris on Wednesday and Thursday.
Member states discussed a proposal from Director General Josef Aschbacher on Europe's future in space exploration.
It sets out a path that can grow step by step, from low Earth orbit to the Moon and then Mars, pairing more European autonomy with international cooperation.
That matters because the International Space Station is heading toward retirement, and Europe still hasn't decided what replaces its presence in orbit.
Delegates also confirmed that the intermediate ministerial meeting will take place in Rome on December fifteenth.
Early preparatory work can start within existing budgets.
The council also reviewed relations with the European Union, including the next seven year E-U budget, the European Competitiveness Fund and the E-U Space Act.
The agency asked for a clear split of roles with Brussels, so that the two don't duplicate work.
In the United States, NASA holds an Artemis briefing at Kennedy Space Center on Friday afternoon.
Administrator Jared Isaacman and program managers will cover Artemis three, now a crewed test in Earth orbit next year, and the goal of landing astronauts on the Moon in twenty twenty eight.
In Washington, senators are pressing SpaceX and the Pentagon over speed limits placed on Starlink terminals used by Ukrainian forces earlier this month.
And the State Department has launched Project Constellation, a five million dollar, two year effort to build space ties with more than seventy emerging space nations.
In India, the space agency has cleared a key separation test for the Gaganyaan crew capsule.
The uncrewed first flight, carrying the robot Vyommitra, is still promised for this year, with a crewed flight targeted for twenty twenty seven.
Brussels and Washington are at odds over satellite spectrum.
The European Commission is preparing to reserve part of the two gigahertz band for direct to device service by European operators.
The American ambassador to the E-U has warned of severe retaliation if non-European constellations are shut out.
The dispute feeds a wider European debate about sovereign access to space.
It also lands as the E-U Space Act moves toward a committee vote in the European Parliament on November tenth.
In Poland, ESA's council named Andrzej Banasiak, who runs Safran Electronics and Defense in Poland, as the agency's Director of Commercialisation and Industry Partnership.
He starts on January first.

At the same time, Prime Minister Donald Tusk is in India with about a hundred business leaders, including the Polish space agency, the companies Scanway and ICEYE, and astronaut Sławosz Uznański-Wiśniewski.
A cooperation agreement between the Polish space agency and India's space agency is planned during the trip, and the delegation heads to Bengaluru on Friday.
In Hungary, the science and technology ministry, which now oversees space, says police have opened investigations into four of its complaints about earlier government contracts.
The same ministry is reviewing inherited space contracts worth roughly eight hundred and twenty to eight hundred and fifty billion forints, some running to twenty forty.
In Türkiye, the twenty twenty seven budget bill raises the space and aviation program to about twenty four point six billion lira, up from eight point seven billion this year.
Close to ninety two billion lira is planned over three years, with the country's first lunar spacecraft aiming for launch in twenty twenty seven.
There was no major new space news today from Uzbekistan, Czechia, Sweden or Greece.
On the business side, SpaceX and Tesla have each set up board committees to study a possible merger, after SpaceX reported revenue of about fourteen point six billion dollars for the quarter.
Rocket Lab says its Neutron rocket won't fly until twenty twenty seven, after flaws turned up in the composite domes of its fuel tanks.
Xona Space Systems raised two hundred and fifty million dollars to build a commercial navigation constellation of about two hundred and fifty eight satellites.
And Hewlett Packard Enterprise plans to send an A-I computer to the Moon on an Astrolab rover, testing language models and image processing on the lunar surface.
Looking ahead, NASA's Artemis briefing is on Friday, October twenty third, the same day the Polish delegation visits Bengaluru.
Novaspace's space summit in Toulouse and the Defence in Space conference in London both run on October twenty seventh and twenty eighth.
Astronauts on the space station are set to make the first of two spacewalks to install new solar arrays on October twenty ninth, with the second on November fifth.
Greece's mission naming call closes October thirtieth.
Americans vote in the midterm elections on November third.
And the European Parliament's industry committee is scheduled to vote on the E-U Space Act on November tenth.
That's the briefing for today.
You'll find the full edition, with links to every source, on the Briefing tab.
Have a good day.

segments.text: Good morning.
It's Wednesday, October twenty first, and here's what's happening in space.
Uzbekistan has signed the Artemis Accords.
NASA has set the rules for its commercial space station competition.
And Europe's space agency is meeting in Paris, with a big ministerial decision coming in December.
Uzbekistan became the seventy seventh country to sign the Artemis Accords.
The signing took place on Monday in Samarkand, during a visit by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the first round of a new strategic partnership dialogue between the two countries.
Uzbekistan's foreign minister said the step opens the door to closer work with NASA, including training for national specialists and the transfer of space technology.
The visit also produced fifty four commercial agreements worth about twelve billion dollars.
They cover critical minerals, aviation, finance and digital technology, and Amazon Leo will work on satellite communications.
Still, Tashkent is keeping its options open.
Two days later it announced wider cooperation with China on artificial intelligence and the digital economy, and it signed a health roadmap with Russia.
In the United States, NASA has finalized its competition for the commercial space stations that will follow the International Space Station.
Proposals are due on December eighth, and awards are expected around April fifteenth next year.
At least two companies will be chosen, with a guaranteed minimum of a hundred million dollars and a ceiling of about thirty four billion over up to fifteen years.
A NASA official also said the agency should ease its requirements further.
The Artemis timeline is firming up.
Artemis Three is now planned as a test in Earth orbit in the middle of twenty twenty seven, and the first crewed landing moves to Artemis Four in early twenty twenty eight.
There was good news for Orion too, as its heat shield performed as expected on Artemis Two.
Japan launched its MMX mission to the Martian moon Phobos, carrying a French and German rover and NASA instruments, with samples due back in twenty thirty one.
And in orbit, the Russian satellite Kosmos twenty six twelve closed to within about five hundred meters of a commercial radar satellite operated by Iceye, whose imagery has supported Ukraine.
It moved away a few days later, but analysts see a pattern of approaches going back to May.
In Europe, the ESA Council is meeting in Paris today and tomorrow, ahead of the ministerial meeting in Rome on December fifteenth.
One of the proposals on the table is a European-led space station in low Earth orbit, which teams led by Airbus and OHB are studying in parallel.
There was a setback for Space Rider.
The full-scale test model was lost when its parafoil failed to open during a drop test, and an investigation is under way.
ESA still expects a first flight in twenty twenty eight.
Four of Europe's biggest telecom groups, Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica and Vodafone, have signed a letter of intent on a European satellite internet service.
In France, lawmakers proposed a symbolic one euro budget line to keep the VORTEX spaceplane in play.
And Spain fast-tracked the funding for its PAZ Two radar satellites.
Closer to home, Greece has opened a public call, running until October thirtieth, to name the mission that will fly its first astronaut, Adrianos Golemis, to the space station next summer.
He'll fly with Vast for about two weeks, alongside France's Thomas Pesquet and Czechia's Aleš Svoboda.
In Poland, a deputy development minister told parliament that the Artemis program lacks financial transparency, and he named Europe's Argonaut lunar lander as Poland's lunar priority.
A Polish Space Agency delegation was in Budapest last week, meeting Hungarian industry and the HUNOR program to talk about secure satellite communications and European cooperation.
And Blue Origin has set up two companies in Kraków to design satellite chips.
Elsewhere in the region, Sweden's SSC signed two Japanese partners in a single week.
And in Türkiye, Fergani put its sixth test satellite into orbit on a SpaceX rideshare, part of a planned constellation of more than two hundred satellites.
On the business side, SpaceX reported third quarter revenue of fourteen point six billion dollars, up a hundred and sixty one percent from a year ago.
Elon Musk says the next Starship flight, planned for November, will try to catch both stages.
Blue Origin is planning more launch pads in Florida, along with expanded manufacturing and more recovery ships, so it can fly New Glenn more often.
And Vast now has astronauts from France, Czechia and Greece booked on the same mission.
Looking ahead, ESA's Director General briefs the media after the Council meeting tomorrow afternoon, and the FAA holds a public meeting on more Blue Origin launches from Cape Canaveral.
On Friday, NASA gives an update on the Artemis program.
Next week, astronauts begin two spacewalks to install the last of the new solar arrays on the space station.
Greece's naming call closes on the thirtieth, and the United States votes in its midterm elections on November third.
That's the briefing for today.
You'll find the full edition, with links to every source, on the Briefing tab.
Have a good day.

Next week, astronauts begin two spacewalks to install the last of the new solar arrays on the space station. Greece's naming call closes on the thirtieth, and the United States votes in its midterm elections on November third.
audio_sections.title: The days ahead

audio_sections.text: That's the briefing for today. You'll find the full edition, with links to every source, on the Briefing tab. Have a good day.
audio_sections.title: Close

sources.title: Uzbekistan, US sign Artemis Accords on exploration of Moon, Mars, comets and asteroids
Artemis Accords
Uzbekistan, US hold first Enhanced Strategic Partnership Dialogue

items.summary: Uzbekistan signed the Artemis Accords in Samarkand on October 19, following talks between Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov and Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the first bilateral Enhanced Strategic Partnership Dialogue. Saidov said the step widens cooperation with NASA, including training national specialists and transferring space technologies.
items.title: Uzbekistan joins the Artemis Accords as 77th signatory
items.why: The signature gives the government commission a politically anchored US option for its human spaceflight decision.

sources.title: Uzbekistan, United States sign 54 agreements worth $12 billion
Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the U.S.-Uzbekistan Business and Investment Council

items.summary: During the Rubio visit, US and Uzbek parties signed 54 agreements worth about $12 billion across critical minerals, finance, aviation, rail, healthcare and digital technology. Amazon Leo will work on satellite communications, and GE Aerospace will supply engines for new Uzbekistan Airways aircraft.
items.title: US and Uzbekistan sign 54 deals worth $12 billion, including satellite communications
items.why: US commercial presence in Tashkent is now broad enough to carry an industrial participation package attached to a spaceflight offer.

sources.title: Uzbekistan and China to Expand Cooperation on AI and Digital Economy
Uzbekistan proposes SCO-2040 strategy and new security coordination mechanism

items.summary: On October 21 Uzbekistan announced expanded AI and digital economy cooperation with China and signed a healthcare roadmap with Russia, a day after proposing an SCO-2040 strategy. The government also announced free AI computing access for startups and universities.
items.title: Tashkent keeps China and Russia tracks running in parallel
items.why: Tashkent is hedging across partners, so a US-aligned offer has to win on ecosystem value, not alignment alone.

sources.title: Polska i Węgry rozmawiają o bezpiecznej łączności satelitarnej

items.summary: Polish Space Agency, Polish interior ministry and Polish industry representatives met Hungarian space industry and HUNOR program representatives in Budapest around October 16 to discuss IRIS2 secure communications, deeper ESA participation and the 2028 to 2034 EU budget. POLSA also presented Poland's regional role at the CEE Space and Defense Day conference in Hungary.
items.title: POLSA delegation in Budapest opens Poland-Hungary track on secure satcom and ESA
items.why: A working Poland-Hungary channel on ESA and EU programs is a practical base for V4 industrial cooperation.

sources.title: US political uncertainty complicates long-term Artemis commitments, Polish minister says

items.summary: In a written reply to a parliamentary question on POLSA's limited role in NASA programs, Deputy Minister of Development and Technology Michał Jaros said Artemis financing lacks transparency and NASA-run programs are costly with limited partner access. He said Poland will keep working closely with ESA and named the Argonaut lunar lander as its lunar priority.
items.title: Polish deputy minister questions Artemis costs, names ESA Argonaut as lunar priority
items.why: Warsaw's supervising ministry is signaling an ESA-first posture, so US-linked offers to Poland need an explicit industrial return story.

sources.title: Blue Origin rozwija działalność w Polsce

items.summary: Blue Origin registered Blue Origin Poland II on September 28 and Blue Origin Poland on October 8, both in Kraków, with job postings for ASIC design, embedded systems and software tied to its TeraWave constellation. One posting targets a 2027 tape-out for a high-throughput modem and digital beamforming chip.
items.title: Blue Origin opens two Polish entities in Kraków for satellite chip work
items.why: A rival station developer is building a Polish engineering footprint it can cite in any Polish partnership conversation.

sources.title: SSC Space and ArkEdge Space sign SSC Space Go and ground segment contract
SSC Space and ElevationSpace sign MoU to explore cooperation

items.summary: SSC Space signed an SSC Space Go and ground segment contract with ArkEdge Space on October 20, four days after an MoU with ElevationSpace to explore cooperation. Both partners are Japanese space startups.
items.title: SSC adds two Japanese partners in a week

sources.title: Προτείνετέ μας το όνομα της αποστολής του πρώτου Έλληνα αστροναύτη!
ESA signs agreement with Vast for first Greek astronaut mission
ESA and Vast expand mission collaborations for the post-ISS era

items.summary: The Hellenic Space Center and the Ministry of Digital Governance opened a public call, closing October 30, to name the Vast-PAM-1 mission that will fly ESA project astronaut Adrianos Golemis to the ISS for two weeks in summer 2027. The seat comes through ESA's September 9 agreement with Vast, and the same flight carries France's Thomas Pesquet and Czechia's Aleš Svoboda.
items.title: Greece launches naming call for first astronaut's Vast-PAM-1 flight
items.why: Greece's first flight is contracted with a competitor, so the opportunity shifts to follow-on missions and station utilization.

sources.title: Fergani'nin altıncı uydusu FRG-100D4 başarıyla yörüngesine yerleşti

items.summary: Fergani's FRG-100D4, a 160 kg satellite with domestically developed avionics, reached a 590 km orbit after launch on SpaceX's Bandwagon-5 rideshare on October 20. It tests navigation and broadband payloads for the planned Uluğ Bey constellation, which targets more than 200 satellites within five years.
items.title: Baykar-linked Fergani puts sixth test satellite in orbit
items.why: Türkiye's private sector is building sovereign navigation and communications capacity quickly, which raises the bar for what a station partnership must add for Ankara.

sources.title: NASA Issues Final RFP for Commercial Space Stations in LEO After ISS Retirement
NASA szuka prywatnego następcy ISS
NASA

global.summary: NASA's final commercial LEO destinations solicitation, issued October 9, sets proposals due December 8 and awards around April 15, 2027 to two or more firms on firm fixed price contracts with a $100 million guaranteed minimum and a $34.06 billion ceiling over up to 15 years. A NASA official said on October 19 that the agency should cut requirements on participants further.
global.title: NASA commercial station competition terms fixed, lighter requirements signaled
global.why: Demonstrated international demand, including sovereign partner commitments, is one of the clearest ways to evidence the commercial viability NASA says it will judge.

sources.title: SpaceX will attempt 1st-ever double Starship rocket catch on next test launch
Felmerült az egyesülés lehetősége a SpaceX-nél és a Teslánál, Musk támogatná

global.summary: SpaceX reported third quarter revenue of $14.6 billion, up 161 percent year on year, and net income of $4.4 billion, with launch contributing $1.8 billion and Starlink and AI segments most of the rest. Elon Musk said Starship Flight 15, targeted for November, will attempt to catch both stages, and both SpaceX and Tesla have formed shareholder committees to study a combination.
global.title: SpaceX posts $14.6 billion quarter, plans double Starship catch
global.why: SpaceX cash generation and Starship cadence set the cost and schedule benchmark for every commercial station and crew transport plan.

sources.title: When will SpaceX and Blue Origin fly to the Moon? NASA reveals lunar lander timelines and an Artemis III update
NASA potwierdza. Osłona termiczna statku Orion zdała egzamin
NASA Update on Artemis Program

global.summary: NASA's updated plan keeps Artemis III as a mid-2027 Earth orbit test of Orion docking with SpaceX and Blue Origin lander test articles, with the first crewed landing on Artemis IV in early 2028. Post-flight analysis found the Orion heat shield performed as expected on Artemis II, with nine small char loss areas against 103 on Artemis I, and NASA leadership briefs on the program October 23.
global.title: Artemis lander timelines firm up, Orion heat shield cleared
global.why: Artemis schedule credibility shapes how Accords signatories weigh NASA-led lunar participation against ESA options.

sources.title: 500 méterre közelített meg egy orosz műhold egy Ukrajnának fontos műholdat
Mit művelt az orosz műhold?

global.summary: Russia's Kosmos 2612 matched orbits with Iceye-X36, a commercial radar satellite owned by Iceye's US subsidiary, and closed to roughly 500 meters around October 16 before moving away by October 19. Analysts tie it to a pattern of Russian approaches to Iceye satellites since May, whose imagery has supported Ukraine since 2022.
global.title: Russian satellite shadows commercial radar satellite used for Ukraine
global.why: Counterspace behavior against commercial assets strengthens the security case inside sovereign space programs across CEE and the Nordics.

sources.title: Media invitation: information session following the 350th ESA Council
ESA Selects Airbus and OHB to Lead European Space Station Studies

items.summary: ESA's 350th Council meets at headquarters in Paris on October 21 and 22, with Director General Josef Aschbacher briefing media on October 22 ahead of the December 15 Intermediate Ministerial Meeting in Rome. Proposals for Rome include a European-led LEO station option now under parallel feasibility studies by Airbus and OHB consortia, with initial development capped at €1 billion per three-year funding period.
items.title: ESA Council meets in Paris ahead of Rome ministerial
items.why: Rome decides whether Europe buys commercial station access, contributes to one, or builds its own, which frames every ESA member state seat and payload conversation.

sources.title: Space Rider Test Model Lost Following Failed Drop Test

items.summary: The full-scale Space Rider test model was lost when its parafoil failed to deploy during the final drop test campaign, the second interruption this year, and an independent investigation is underway. ESA still expects a first flight in 2028 but has moved the target from the first to the second quarter.
items.title: Space Rider test model lost in failed drop test
items.why: Europe's own reusable microgravity return capability slips again, which keeps European researchers dependent on partner platforms.

sources.title: Megvan az aláírás: jöhet az európai műholdas internet, nagy nevek dolgozhatnak rajta
Mobilní operátoři

items.summary: Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica and Vodafone signed a letter of intent to reserve spectrum and jointly provide ground infrastructure for a European satellite internet service, with the constellation partner still unselected. The effort sits alongside the EU's IRIS2 program, and no formal link has been stated.
items.title: Four European telecom groups sign intent on sovereign satellite service
items.why: Sovereignty arguments are now driving private European procurement as well as public programs.

sources.title: French MPs propose symbolic €1 budget line for VORTEX spaceplane

items.summary: French members of parliament proposed a symbolic one euro budget line for the VORTEX spaceplane during the budget debate. The move keeps a national reusable vehicle option visible while ESA debates Europe's post-ISS human spaceflight path.
items.title: French lawmakers propose token budget line for VORTEX spaceplane

sources.title: Španělsko schválilo předčasné financování špionážních družic PAZ 2

items.summary: Spain approved early release of funds for the PAZ 2 radar reconnaissance satellites. It is another European government accelerating sovereign defense space spending.
items.title: Spain fast-tracks funding for PAZ 2 reconnaissance satellites

sources.title: 'Enduring partners of choice'. Central Asian nations, US agree to expand ties at Samarkand meeting
Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Uzbekistan Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov at the C5+1 Ministerial

items.summary: Foreign ministers of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan met Secretary Rubio in Samarkand on October 19 and issued a joint statement on trade routes, critical minerals, energy, security and trusted technology. The statement does not mention space.
items.title: C5+1 ministers in Samarkand frame the US as a long-term regional partner
items.why: US political attention to Central Asia makes Kazakhstan and its neighbors plausible next Artemis Accords candidates and opens room for US-aligned human spaceflight offers.

sources.title: Velitelství Vesmírných sil

items.summary: Reporting indicates the US Space Force component in the Middle East may expand to five times its current size. It signals a heavier US military space footprint in the Gulf region.
items.title: US Space Force Middle East command may grow fivefold

sources.title: MMX lifts off to Mars's moon Phobos
JAXA's MMX Enroute to Mars To Return Samples of Phobos
Japanese MMX mission launches to study Martian moons

items.summary: JAXA launched the MMX mission on the first H3-24L from Tanegashima on October 19 UTC, carrying the French and German Idefix rover and NASA instruments, with Phobos samples due back in 2031. ESA supplied deep space communication equipment and Estrack ground station support under its Science Program.
items.title: Japan launches MMX Phobos sample return with European support

sources.title: Blue Origin plánuje na Floridě obří expanzi
What's Happening in Space Policy October 18-24, 2026

items.summary: Blue Origin plans additional Florida launch pads, a manufacturing expansion and more recovery vessels to increase the New Glenn flight rate. The FAA holds a public meeting on October 22 on its draft environmental assessment for more Blue Origin launches at Cape Canaveral.
items.title: Blue Origin plans new Florida pads to raise New Glenn cadence
items.why: Higher New Glenn cadence matters for Orbital Reef and Blue Moon schedules, both competitors for the same post-ISS and lunar budgets.

strategy.summary: Angola's National Space Strategy 2016-2025 was approved by Presidential Decree No. 85/17 and is implemented by GGPEN, the national space program management office under the telecommunications ministry. It is built on five axes: space infrastructure, training and promotion, industry and technology, international positioning, and organization and cooperation. Its horizon has passed and no successor strategy was found, though the government cited it in October 2025 when announcing the conversion of GGPEN into an Angolan Space Agency.

strategy.summary: The UAE Cabinet approved the National Space Strategy 2031 in March 2026, aligned with the We the UAE 2031 and UAE Centennial 2071 visions. It shifts the emphasis from flagship science missions toward a commercial space economy, investment attraction, international partnerships and market access, and competitive national infrastructure. The headline aim is to place the UAE among the world's top 10 space economies by 2031. It succeeds the National Space Strategy 2030 adopted in 2019.

strategy.summary: The Statement on Space, released in July 2026 by the Minister for Industry and Innovation and Minister for Science, sets the federal government's vision for lifting national space industrial capability, moving into higher value work and expanding into global markets. It identifies five focus areas and the levers government can use to coordinate demand, investment and regulation. The Australian Space Agency is consulting industry, academia and government on detailed actions expected later in 2026. It sits alongside the earlier Australian Civil Space Strategy 2019 to 2028 and a new Statement of Expectations to the agency.

strategy.summary: Belgium has no single published long-term national space strategy document. Federal space policy is set through the Council of Ministers decision of 23 December 2025 on Belgian space programming for 2026 to 2030, which funded the ESA subscriptions made at the November 2025 Bremen ministerial and introduced defense co-financing of ESA participation. BELSPO designs and implements the policy around science, societal use, industrial development and economic return. The decision mandates a strategic review by 2028 to define future Belgian space policy.

strategy.summary: Bulgaria has no adopted national space strategy. In its 2025 statements to UN COPUOS the government said drafting a National Space Strategy and a National Space Program is its top short-term priority, alongside domestic space legislation and the creation of a national space agency. Space policy is coordinated by the Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation, and in practice is framed by the European Cooperating State Agreement with ESA (renewed in 2022), EU space program participation, and the Artemis Accords (joined 2023). A draft update to the Innovation Strategy for Smart Specialisation 2021-2027 adds a national priority on space and dual-use technologies (public consultation closed 20 September 2026).

The current PNAE covers 2022 to 2031 and was approved at the end of 2021. strategy.summary: Chile's National Space Policy was approved by Supreme Decree No. 30 of July 2024 and cleared by the Comptroller General in March 2025, succeeding the 2014-2020 policy. It rests on two central objectives, the sustainable development of national space capabilities and the integrated management of space for national security and socioeconomic progress, organized around six strategic axes. Implementation runs largely through the National Satellite System (SNSat) operated by the Chilean Air Force and the National Space Center in Cerrillos, which opened in December 2025.

strategy.summary: White paper issued by the State Council Information Office in January 2022 that reviews progress since 2016 and sets out space tasks for the following five years under the long-term aim of building China into a space power. It covers launch vehicles, space infrastructure, human spaceflight, lunar and planetary exploration, space governance and international cooperation. No successor space white paper was found in this run, and current direction is carried forward by the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026 to 2030) adopted in March 2026, which shifts space toward a market-oriented industry with large constellations, reusable launchers and crewed lunar preparations.

strategy.summary: Colombia's most recent adopted space policy is CONPES 3983 of January 2020, which set enabling conditions for the space sector to support national productivity and competitiveness, with an action plan that closed in December 2021. It called for reforming the Colombian Space Commission, reducing barriers for private entry, filing orbit and spectrum resources with the ITU, and commercializing defense satellite capabilities. As of 2025 the Colombian Space Commission reported to UN COPUOS that it was drafting a new National Space Policy to define national space governance and institutions, and no successor policy had been identified as adopted by this date.

government.notes: Cyprus has a full presidential system in which the President is both head of state and head of government, and the deputy ministries report directly to the President. Space policy is led by the Deputy Ministry of Research, Innovation and Digital Policy, with its Department of Electronic Communications designated by Council of Ministers decision as the Cyprus Space Office, rather than a standalone space agency. Funding flows mainly through the Deputy Ministry budget (including the ESA contribution) and the Research and Innovation Foundation, while the House of Representatives ratifies treaties such as the ESA Association Agreement. The May 2026 parliamentary elections did not change the executive, as the President's term runs to 2028.

strategy.summary: Approved by the government in October 2025, the plan sets the long-term vision for Czechia as an active and internationally recognized space actor that uses space technologies for the economy, society and security. It defines seven strategic goals and seven competence platforms, from satellites up to 500 kg and scientific instruments to Earth observation data processing and space security and defense. It also frames the national Czech Path to Space project, including a Czech astronaut mission to the ISS expected around 2027 to 2028. Coordination of space activities moved from the Ministry of Transport to the Ministry of Industry and Trade on 1 March 2026.

strategy.summary: Germany's national space strategy was adopted by the federal cabinet on 27 September 2023, replacing the 2010 strategy, and treats space infrastructure as critical infrastructure for Germany and Europe. It sets nine fields of action ranging from European and international cooperation and New Space growth to security, sustainability, research and exploration. Since 2025 federal civil space policy has been consolidated in the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space (BMFTR), which told the Bundestag in November 2025 that a decision on rewriting the strategy will follow once its new space department is fully established. A separate Space Security Strategy was presented in cabinet in November 2025.

strategy.summary: Spain has no single adopted national space strategy. Its civil space policy rests on the Spanish Space Agency (AEE), created by Royal Decree 158/2023 under the joint authority of the Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities and the Ministry of Defense, and on the 2022 Aerospace PERTE investment plan. On the security side, the 2019 National Aerospace Security Strategy, adopted under the National Security Council, still frames policy. In 2023 the science minister set a Space Law and a National Space Plan as AEE objectives, and the government has committed 455 million euros a year to ESA through 2030.

strategy.summary: Hungary adopted its first national space strategy in 2021, aiming to use the space sector as a driver of innovation and growth, to strengthen the country's international role, and to build the knowledge base and infrastructure for the sector. Its flagship projects were national satellite and ground segment capabilities and the HUNOR astronaut program, which flew a Hungarian astronaut to the ISS on Axiom Mission 4 in June 2025. After the May 2026 change of government, space coordination moved to the new Ministry of Science and Technology, which has named renewal of the strategy as its first space task, together with closer ESA ties and a new regulatory and institutional framework.

government.notes: Space decisions in Indonesia are presidential, set through presidential regulations and approved through the DPR budget process. BRIN is the single implementing body for civil space research and reports directly to the President, while defense space and satellite communications regulation sit with the Ministry of Defense and Komdigi. Institutional arrangements for the Biak spaceport were still under discussion with KemenPAN-RB and other ministries in early 2026. The next presidential and legislative elections are scheduled for 2029.

strategy.summary: Indonesia's space policy rests on Law No. 21 of 2013 on Space Activities and the 2017 presidential master plan that sets long term targets to 2040 for space science, remote sensing, space technology, launch and commercial space activities. Since the former space agency LAPAN was merged into the National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN) in 2021, space research and implementation sit inside BRIN. The master plan is evaluated every five years, and BRIN officials stated in early 2026 that some targets need to be redefined to be more adaptive and realistic. Current priorities are a national spaceport at Biak, Papua, and domestically built Earth observation satellites focused on food security.

strategy.summary: Cabinet-approved policy that opens the full space value chain to non-government entities and assigns distinct roles to the Department of Space, ISRO, IN-SPACe and NSIL. ISRO is refocused on research, advanced technology and human spaceflight, IN-SPACe authorizes and promotes non-government space activities, and NSIL commercializes mature systems. strategy.summary: Ireland's first national space strategy, launched in June 2019, is enterprise focused and aims to grow Irish companies' participation in ESA and EU programs. Its horizon ended in 2025, with 15 of 19 priority actions completed and a final progress report under way. The department has begun a scoping exercise for a successor National Space Strategy for Enterprise, which will include public consultation. Ireland signed the Artemis Accords in May 2026.

government.notes: Strategic direction rests with the Supreme Leader, while the civil program is set by the Supreme Space Council under the President and run by the ICT ministry through ISA and ISRC. Funding comes through the annual budget law approved by the Majlis and through defense channels for the IRGC track, which operates largely outside civil oversight. Mojtaba Khamenei was named Supreme Leader on 8 March 2026 after Ali Khamenei was killed on 28 February, and he has not appeared in verified video or audio since, so his health and role are disputed. The war that began in February 2026 is unresolved as of this date, with a US naval blockade and intermittent strikes, which adds uncertainty to budgets and leadership.

strategy.summary: Iran's space activity is governed by a 10-year roadmap drafted by the ICT ministry and approved by the Supreme Space Council in 2022, which aims to make Iran a regional hub for space technology. Priorities are Earth observation, communications and positioning satellites, sovereign launch capability, and reaching geostationary orbit. The program has continued during the 2026 war despite strikes on facilities, including the Iranian Space Research Center in Tehran. A civil track under the Iranian Space Agency runs in parallel with a military track under the IRGC Aerospace Force.

strategy.summary: Approved at the 29th COMINT meeting on 14 May 2026, the DSPSN is Italy's first comprehensive national planning framework for space and implements the Government Guidelines on Space and Aerospace approved by COMINT in late 2024. It sets priorities for the next decade along four axes: research and benefits for society, industrial competitiveness, governance and regulation, and international cooperation. It treats space as a domain of strategic competition and calls for a national space security strategy, a critical space technologies plan and operational security and defense capabilities. It operates within Law No. 89 of 2025 on the space economy.

strategy.summary: Kyrgyzstan has no published national space strategy, space law or space agency as of this run. Space activity is driven by presidential and Cabinet of Ministers decisions, chiefly a 2026 Cabinet resolution creating the state company Kyrgyz Sputnik (renamed Kyrgyz Asman in June 2026) under the Ministry of Water Resources, Agriculture and Processing Industry. strategy.summary: Mongolia has no adopted standalone national space strategy. Space policy rests on the Vision 2050 long term development policy, which calls for integrating space technology into disaster management and building domestic research capacity, and on the Government Action Program 2024 to 2028, which lists a national communications satellite as the first of 14 mega projects. A National Space Council was set up in 2022 to coordinate policy, with its secretariat in the digital development ministry. A three stage space technology development concept for 2020 to 2049, proposed by the National University of Mongolia, the Academy of Sciences and the Mongolian Space Technology Association, has not been adopted as official strategy.

strategy.summary: The Long-Term Space Agenda, prepared on the advice of the Netherlands Space Office and endorsed by the cabinet in February 2025, replaced the earlier three-year policy cycle tied to ESA ministerial conferences. It sets six missions spanning security, climate, science, satellite data, industry and international law. A 2017 to 2024 policy evaluation found the missions insufficiently concrete, and in January 2026 the cabinet committed to prioritize them. The Netherlands Space Office was renamed the Netherlands Space Agency in March 2026 with a stronger mandate.

strategy.summary: Oman's National Space Policy and Executive Program is a ten year framework for 2023 to 2033 that aims to make Oman a regional hub for space applications. It rests on four pillars (economic diversification, national security, capacity building and environmental stewardship) and prioritizes the downstream sector as the entry point. Implementation runs in three phases, from preparation and legal frameworks, to priority projects, to expansion and sustainability, through 14 key projects and 8 quick wins. The ministry reported that 2023 to 2025 achievements included growth to about 26 space companies and over 400 sector jobs.

strategy.summary: Pakistan's first National Space Policy was approved by the federal cabinet in December 2023 and sets the country's first legal and regulatory framework for space activities. It frames space as a tool for socioeconomic development and national security, commits to peaceful use, and opens the market to public-private partnerships and foreign low Earth orbit communications providers. SUPARCO implements, monitors and revises the policy, and the Pakistan Space Activities Regulatory Board licenses operators under rules issued in 2024. The policy sits beside the longer running Space Program 2040, which drives a fast satellite launch cadence built mainly with Chinese partners.

strategy.summary: The Philippine Space Act, approved on 8 August 2019, embeds the Philippine Space Development and Utilization Policy and created the Philippine Space Agency (PhilSA) as the central body for space policy and programs. The policy aims to make the country space-capable and space-faring within a decade, organized around six key development areas. Implementation runs through PhilSA, whose Director General holds Cabinet rank and serves as Presidential Adviser on Space Matters, with the Earth observation satellite MULA as the current flagship mission expected to launch in late 2026.

strategy.summary: Portugal Space 2030 was approved by the Council of Ministers on 15 February 2018 together with the draft Space Law, and set the national strategy for space to 2030. It aims to grow a space economy built on data, services and infrastructure, using the Atlantic position of the Azores for launch, return and ground station activities. In 2025 the government set up a Space Interministerial Working Group that shaped a record ESA subscription, and the 2026 agenda centers on the Santa Maria spaceport, reentry operations and the Atlantic Constellation with Spain. No formal successor strategy had been published as of this file.

strategy.summary: Rwanda's National Space Policy, dated March 2025, sets the goal of a resilient space sector by 2035 that contributes to economic growth and quality of life. It is organized around the principles Build, Grow, Collaborate and Inspire and six policy areas (economic development, international cooperation, education and capacity building, sustainability and self-reliance, regulatory framework, governance). The program is civilian led and implemented mainly through the Rwanda Space Agency, which regulates and coordinates national space activities.

strategy.summary: Singapore has not published a national space strategy document. The policy basis is the mandate of the National Space Agency of Singapore (NSAS), established on 1 April 2026 under the trade and industry ministry, which took over the Office for Space Technology and Industry (OSTIn) and has five pillars: national space capabilities, R&D, industry, international partnerships and space legislation. Operational guidance comes from the 2024 Guidelines for Singapore Related Space Activities, and funding from the S$210 million Space Technology Development Program set aside since 2022. Official statements say Singapore does not prioritize launch capability because of land constraints.

government.notes: Serbia has no space agency, so space decisions run through the Government and individual ministries, with the Ministry of Science as the de facto lead and funder through its research budget. International commitments are driven by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Artemis Accords, 2026) and sector bodies (RHMZ for EUMETSAT, BioSense for Copernicus). The political setting is in flux: President Vucic resigned on 27 September 2026 to run for Prime Minister, Speaker Ana Brnabic is acting President, the National Assembly is dissolved ahead of the 25 October 2026 snap election, and a presidential election must follow within three months. Prime Minister Djuro Macut (in office since 16 April 2025) leads the government until a new one is formed.

strategy.summary: The Cabinet approved the 15-year National Space Master Plan 2023-2037 in December 2022, alongside a National Communication Satellite Policy. The plan aims to build a space economy that supports national security, prosperity and sustainability through eight strategies covering security, economy and industry, innovation, technology, exploration and international cooperation. strategy.summary: Taiwan's space policy is set by the Phase III National Space Program, announced in 2019 for 2019 to 2028 with an expected cost of NT$25.1 billion and a target of at least one satellite launch per year. It shifts Taiwan from single satellites to constellations, with domestic optical, SAR and low Earth orbit communications satellites, launch vehicles and a national launch site. The Taiwan Space Agency, an administrative corporation under the National Science and Technology Council, implements the program. TASA describes its two main goals as strengthening national security and promoting the space industry.

strategy.summary: Executive Order 14369, signed on December 18, 2025, sets national space policy across civil exploration, national security, commercial development and space nuclear power. It fixes deadlines for a crewed Moon return and a permanent lunar outpost, directs the Secretary of War to implement a space security strategy, and gives commercial solutions preference in federal space acquisition. It revoked EO 14056 and with it the National Space Council, placing coordination with the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology.

strategy.summary: Decision 169/QD-TTg, signed by the Prime Minister on 4 February 2021, sets Vietnam's space science and technology strategy through 2030 and builds on the 2006 national space technology strategy. It targets a mid-level position in space science and technology in Southeast Asia by 2030, mastery of small high-resolution Earth observation satellite technology, replacement of the VINASAT communication satellites and a large expansion of the space workforce. At the March 2026 inauguration of the Vietnam National Space Center, the government restated these targets and said it is moving toward a national space law.

The Land has no dedicated space office or strategy.

DEU-TH.profile: Space activity in Thuringia is concentrated in Jena's optics and photonics cluster. USA-MO.profile: Missouri's largest space-related presence is the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, which opened its roughly $1.7 billion Next NGA West campus in north St. Louis on September 26, 2025, replacing its older downtown site. Boeing maintains a major defense and space workforce in St. Louis, the historic home of McDonnell Aircraft's Mercury and Gemini spacecraft, and the state's aerospace supplier base contributes to NASA programs. Space research includes the McDonnell Center for the Space Sciences at Washington University in St. Louis and student satellite work at Missouri University of Science and Technology in Rolla, whose M-SAT launched in 2024.

Stennis Space Center, the main U.S. rocket propulsion test site, where every RS-25 engine for the Space Launch System is tested (new production L3Harris engines were hot fired in 2025). Stennis hosts more than 50 federal, state, academic and commercial tenants, with commercial test operations by Relativity Space (the largest commercial footprint, including the R Complex expansion for Terran R) and Rocket Lab (Archimedes engine testing on the A-3 stand).

USA-MT.profile: Montana has limited space activity, centered on Montana State University in Bozeman. The Space Science and Engineering Laboratory builds student and faculty space hardware, including CubeSats, and the university's solar physics group works on solar observation missions. The Montana Space Grant Consortium is hosted at the university, and the Montana Department of Commerce promotes the state's photonics and optics industry, much of it clustered around Bozeman.

USA-NC.name: North Carolina
USA-NC.profile: North Carolina has no NASA center, launch site or spaceport, and its space activity is mainly academic and early-stage commercial. NC State University in Raleigh administers the NASA-funded North Carolina Space Grant, UNC Chapel Hill runs the Skynet robotic telescope network, and the Pisgah Astronomical Research Institute occupies the former NASA Rosman satellite tracking station (opened 1962), whose property was listed for sale in 2025 while the institute continues to operate. Durham startup Extellis, a Duke University spinout, raised a $6.8 million seed round in 2025 to build synthetic aperture radar imaging satellites and is preparing its first orbital demonstration. Most state aerospace investment, including JetZero's planned aircraft plant at Piedmont Triad International Airport, is in aviation rather than space.

USA-ND.name: North Dakota
USA-ND.profile: Grand Forks Air Force Base hosts a Space Development Agency operations center for its low Earth orbit constellation, supported by a General Dynamics Mission Systems ground contract, and a satellite test and checkout center due for completion in 2026. In April 2026 Senator John Hoeven proposed a further 250 million dollar Space Operations Center at the base to support the Space Force and the National Reconnaissance Office (not yet approved). Cavalier Space Force Station operates the PARCS missile warning and space tracking radar with the 10th Space Warning Squadron, and the University of North Dakota runs a Department of Space Studies.

Offutt Air Force Base near Bellevue hosts the Air Force 557th Weather Wing, whose 2nd Weather Group produces space weather products and runs the military solar observatory network. University of Nebraska Lincoln engineering students built a CubeSat launched to the International Space Station on a NASA resupply mission in 2024.

The University of New Hampshire Space Science Center in Morse Hall, Durham, builds instruments for NASA satellite and sounding rocket missions and runs a cosmic ray neutron monitor on Mount Washington. The New Jersey Institute of Technology in Newark runs the Center for Solar-Terrestrial Research and an Institute for Space Weather Sciences, and Rowan University in Glassboro was the first New Jersey university to send a satellite to space under a NASA CubeSat program. The New Jersey Economic Development Authority is developing an $8.6 million Aerospace Innovation Center in Atlantic County, focused mainly on aviation.

NASA's White Sands Test Facility and White Sands Missile Range support propulsion testing and flight operations. Kirtland Air Force Base in Albuquerque hosts the AFRL Space Vehicles Directorate and the Space Rapid Capabilities Office, alongside Sandia and Los Alamos national laboratories and Rocket Lab's space solar cell production, which received CHIPS Act funding.

L3Harris designs and builds high resolution imaging payloads for government and commercial satellites in Rochester, and Moog completed a major expansion of its space actuation and avionics manufacturing in East Aurora in 2025. NASA ended the lease of the Goddard Institute for Space Studies at Columbia University in 2025, and its staff have worked remotely since June 2025. Beyond Reach Labs opened a 16,000 square foot Brooklyn facility for deployable spacecraft solar arrays in September 2026.

USA-OH.name: Ohio
USA-OH.profile: Ohio's space role centers on NASA Glenn Research Center in Cleveland and Brook Park, which leads propulsion, power and communications research, and its Neil Armstrong Test Facility near Sandusky, home of the Space Environments Complex. Wright-Patterson Air Force Base hosts Air Force Research Laboratory headquarters, the National Air and Space Intelligence Center and the Space Force's National Space Intelligence Center, activated in 2022. Glenn and the Armstrong Test Facility employed about 600 fewer civil servants and contractors in January 2026 than a year earlier after buyouts and contract cancellations. In September 2026 Governor DeWine formed a steering group, chaired by the Ohio Department of Development, to pursue the planned U.S. Space Academy.

The South Carolina Space Grant Consortium is based at the College of Charleston, whose students' ultraviolet imaging payload flew to the International Space Station in April 2026 and whose CubeSat payload launched in July 2026. Coastal Carolina University is building the state's first university-run CubeSat and requested $450,000 in state funds for its launch in January 2026, and Clemson University signed a Space Act Agreement with NASA Johnson Space Center in April 2024. In September 2026 Governor Ferguson created the 23-member Washington Space Council by Executive Order 26-04, staffed by the state Department of Commerce.
